newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi verdict in case of British nurses next week.
newsitem.headline: Saudi verdict in case of British nurses next week.

text.p: A verdict in the trial of two British nurses accused of killing an Australian colleague in Saudi Arabia is expected in a week, sources close to the case said on Monday.

If Deborah Parry and Lucille McLauchlan were found guilty of any charge, the case would go through an elaborate appeals system in the kingdom, which applies strict Islamic laws including beheading by the sword for murderers, drug smugglers and rapists.
The women say they are innocent and have withdrawn confessions which they said they were forced to sign.

The sources said the understanding from the Islamic sharia court in the eastern Saudi city of Khobar, which adjourned on Sunday to deliberate on the verdict, was that a ruling would probably be issued next Sunday.
It was not yet clear whether the relatives of defendants Parry, 38, and McLauchlan, 31, would attend the hearing, the sources added.
Saudi newspapers reported on Monday that the verdict would be issued next week, but did not specify the date.

A statement from the defence lawyers at the law firm of Salah al-Hejailan sent to Reuters on Sunday said: "It was not clear from what has taken place in the sharia court (on Sunday) whether the judges will dismiss the case or uphold the confessions or submit the case to a higher court."
If found not guilty of any charge the two women -- in prison since December -- would walk free, the sources said.

If found guilty of any charge -- which could be manslaughter, premeditated, unpremeditated or accidental murder -- the court would pronounce the sentence it deemed appropriate at the same time as the verdict.
"The court decides what the charge is while deliberating the verdict," one source said.
Parry and McLauchlan are accused of murdering Yvonne Gilford, 55, last December at a military medical complex in the eastern Saudi city of Dhahran where they all worked.
Lawyers representing Gilford's family said on Sunday the court rejected new defence evidence.
"The court has adjourned and both parties will be notified of the verdict at a later stage," Usama al-Sulayem from the International Law Firm told Reuters by telephone from Riyadh.
"There will no more hearings, no lawyers, no documents," he said. The court would issue the verdict at a closed session.

Defence lawyers said they presented new evidence on Sunday which they hoped would undermine the right of the victim's family to demand the death penalty if the two women were found guilty of killing Gilford.

According to Saudi law the victim's immediate family -- her mother Muriel and brother Frank -- have authority to demand the death penalty if the defendants are found guilty and the court rules the death penalty is appropriate.
Frank Gilford, who lives in Australia, has repeatedly said he prefers the maximum sentence. His mother lives in an Australian nursing home. Neither has attended any of the court sessions.
Defence lawyers said they gave the court a copy of a medical report showing the victim's mother was not mentally competent, making her unable to agree with her son's call for execution.
Lawyers in Australia representing the nurses said Muriel Gilford suffered from Alzheimer's disease.

Legal experts in Riyadh said that under Saudi law, a call for the death penalty by a victim's family must be unanimous. They said that if Muriel Gilford was mentally incapacitated, Frank Gilford could not make the decision alone.
